identification.summary: PROMETHIUM is an espionage-focused activity group that other vendors call StrongPity (also SmallPity) and that MITRE describes as active since at least 2012, operating globally with a heavy emphasis on Turkish targets [S3]. Vendors also track it as APT-C-41 [S4]. The Microsoft name Magenta Dust could not be confirmed on a Microsoft page in fact-check searches (only a third-party aggregator lists it).
identification.firstObserved: 2012 (MITRE: active since at least 2012) [S3]; first public reporting October 2016 [S8]
identification.notes: In December 2016 Microsoft reported PROMETHIUM and NEODYMIUM as separate groups that both used the same Flash zero-day (CVE-2016-4117); MITRE notes similarity to NEODYMIUM from overlapping victim and campaign characteristics [S3][S6]. Do not merge NEODYMIUM facts into this profile. The 2016 Microsoft blog was not opened directly; its content is taken from secondary coverage [S6][S7].

attribution.basis: Several reports state it is unclear which country backs StrongPity, and ESET attributes individual campaigns to the StrongPity cluster (not to a state) on code similarity and a shared code-signing certificate [S4][S5]. A Turkiye origin attributed to Microsoft's naming table could not be verified. No government attribution was found.

objectives: Espionage: MITRE characterizes the group as espionage-focused [S3]. ESET describes a StrongPity Android backdoor that records calls and collects SMS, call logs, contacts and location, consistent with surveillance of individuals [S4].

regions: Colombia, India, Canada and Vietnam (StrongPity3 samples) [S2]
Europe, Northern Africa, Canada and Asia (per Cyble) [S10]
targeting.notes: Microsoft reported in 2016 that PROMETHIUM targeted individuals in Turkey and several European countries using a Flash zero-day [S6]. The 2016 campaign delivered trojanized WinRAR and TrueCrypt installers to users in Belgium and Italy [S8]. ESET assessed the 2022-2023 Android campaign as likely very narrowly targeted and had identified no victims in its telemetry [S4]. Target sectors are not stated in the sources reviewed; targeting appears to be of individuals interested in specific software.

capabilities.summary: Main tooling documented by vendors: Truvasys first-stage malware, bundled with trojanized utilities such as WinRAR, WinUtils, TrueCrypt and SanDisk tools [S2][S10]; Myntor malware reported by Microsoft in 2016 [S6]. Trojanized installers have also included Firefox and VPNpro lookalikes, and in some cases the installer reconfigures Windows Defender before dropping malware [S2]. Alien Labs reported 2018-2019 use of a trojanized WinBox router-management installer and WinRAR, with malware rebuilt after public reporting [S9]. Talos could not confirm the initial vector for StrongPity3 and suspected watering-hole or in-path request interception, citing earlier Citizen Lab reporting [S2]. ESET documented an Android backdoor in a repackaged Telegram app (Android/StrongPity.A) with 11 dynamically triggered modules that record calls and collect SMS, call logs and contacts, and with accessibility and notification access it reads notifications from messaging apps [S4]. PROMETHIUM used the Flash zero-day CVE-2016-4117 before public disclosure [S6].

campaigns.name: Trojanized WinRAR and TrueCrypt watering-hole campaign
campaigns.summary: Attacks in mid-2016 against users in Belgium and Italy used watering holes to deliver malicious WinRAR and TrueCrypt installers; first public reporting on StrongPity came in October 2016 [S8].

campaigns.name: Twin Flash zero-day attacks (PROMETHIUM and NEODYMIUM)
campaigns.summary: Microsoft reported that PROMETHIUM and NEODYMIUM, as two distinct groups, exploited the same Flash Player zero-day (CVE-2016-4117) against individuals in Turkey and Europe; PROMETHIUM used Truvasys and Myntor [S6][S7].

campaigns.name: Network-injection redirects in Turkey and Syria (related reporting)
campaigns.summary: Citizen Lab reported deep packet inspection middleboxes on Turk Telekom's network redirecting users downloading legitimate Windows software to spyware-laden versions; the report as summarized does not name the operator, and Talos cites it when discussing StrongPity's possible in-path interception [S11][S2].

campaigns.name: Rebuilt StrongPity malware and trojanized WinBox installer
campaigns.summary: Alien Labs reported a previously unreported campaign running from the second half of 2018 into mid-2019, with new malware and infrastructure, trojanized WinBox, WinRAR and other software; the malware appeared rebuilt in response to public reporting [S9].

campaigns.name: StrongPity3 global expansion
campaigns.summary: Cisco Talos reported StrongPity3 samples targeting victims in Colombia, India, Canada and Vietnam, and identified about 30 new C2 domains [S2].

campaigns.name: Shagle lookalike site and Syrian e-government app
campaigns.summary: ESET reported a copycat Shagle website, in use since 2021 with HTML copied in November 2021, distributing a trojanized Telegram APK; ESET linked it to StrongPity via code similarity and a signing certificate shared with a 2021 Android app that impersonated a Syrian e-government application [S4][S5].

campaigns.name: ESET public disclosure of StrongPity Android backdoor
campaigns.summary: ESET published its analysis on 2023-01-10 of Android/StrongPity.A in the repackaged Telegram app; it could not confirm the initial vector and suspected spear-phishing, smishing or platform messages [S4][S5].

diamond.adversary: Cluster tracked by Microsoft as PROMETHIUM, by others as StrongPity, SmallPity and APT-C-41; operator identity and sponsor are not established in the sources reviewed [S3][S4].
diamond.capability: Truvasys and Myntor malware, trojanized installers of common utilities, a Flash zero-day (2016), and an Android backdoor in a repackaged Telegram app [S2][S4][S6].
diamond.infrastructure: Fake software and copycat websites for lures, including a Shagle lookalike site [S4]; about 30 new C2 domains identified by Talos in 2020 [S2]; Bitdefender (via secondary reporting) described a three-tier C2 design [S12].
diamond.victim: Individuals in Turkey, Syria, Belgium, Italy, and later Colombia, India, Canada and Vietnam [S2][S3][S8].
diamond.socioPolitical: Heavy emphasis on Turkish targets and early Turkey/Syria focus suggest regional interest; motive beyond espionage is not stated in sources [S3].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints via trojanized installers, Adobe Flash (2016), router-admin software users (WinBox), and Android devices [S4][S6][S9].

gaps: Sponsor is not established; the Magenta Dust name and any Turkiye origin could not be verified against a Microsoft page; no government attribution found.

Microsoft's December 2016 blog, Kaspersky's 2016 report, Bitdefender's report and the Citizen Lab PDF were not opened directly; content comes from search summaries or secondary coverage. MITRE and Talos pages could not be fetched (host unresolved); their content comes from search summaries.
No 2024-2026 StrongPity reporting was found in the searches run; current activity level is unknown.
Whether the Citizen Lab Bad Traffic redirections are attributable to this cluster is not established in sources reviewed.
Initial access vectors for most campaigns are unconfirmed (ESET and Talos both state this).
Target sectors are not documented; victims reported are mostly individuals.
Overlap and relationship with NEODYMIUM remains described only as similarity; not resolved.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Operational environment: the cluster operates against individuals and small organizations via trojanized popular utilities and mobile apps, not against hardened networks [S4][S8]. Adversary characteristics: espionage-focused, long-running (since at least 2012), re-tools after public reporting [S3][S9]. MLCOA: continued trojanized installer and repackaged-app lures against individuals in the Turkey/Syria region and diaspora, with opportunistic wider reach as seen in StrongPity3 [S2][S4]. MDCOA: use of a zero-day against Windows or mobile software, as with the 2016 Flash exploit [S6]. Candidate indicators: unofficial download sites or lookalike app sites, installers that alter Windows Defender settings, apps requesting accessibility and notification access, and new C2 domains tied to Truvasys/StrongPity families [S2][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: personnel travelling to or communicating with Turkey, Syria or Europe-based contacts using personal devices are the plausible exposure, since reported victims are individuals [S4][S8]. Authorities: any response against personal devices or commercial app sources involves legal and policy review outside this source set. Mission assurance: enforce software-sourcing controls (official repositories only, checksums for utilities like WinRAR and router tools) and mobile sideloading restrictions [S2][S4][S9]. Coordination: share indicators through established intelligence and cyber-defense channels and track vendor naming (PROMETHIUM, StrongPity) to deconflict reporting.
